idiom_name: split / base-case solve / combine, driven by a task pool with join (structure, not a class)
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: a recursive routine that (1) tests the base case and solves the trivial subproblem directly and sequentially, (2) splits the remaining problem into independent subproblems of the same form, (3) forks the subproblems to the runtime's task pool and joins them, and (4) combines the partial results. The four roles stay separable - splitter, base-case solver, combiner and the scheduler that maps the logical decomposition onto real threads (work stealing, futures, task scopes) - and the split/combine pair is chosen so that the parallel result is identical to the sequential one. The cut-off is part of the design, not a tuning detail: below it the fork/join overhead exceeds the leaf work.
code_sketch:
solve(problem):
    if base_case(problem):
        return leaf_solve(problem)          # sequential cut-off
    left, right = split(problem)            # independent subproblems
    lres, rres = fork_join(lambda: solve(left), lambda: solve(right))
    return combine(lres, rres)              # merge in the parent only
pitfalls: Omitting the cut-off: every fork/join costs a task object, a wake-up and a join, which dwarfs the leaf work for small subproblems.
Combining through shared mutable state instead of the returned pair - the two branches then stop being independent and the result becomes scheduling-dependent.
A join that does not propagate failure or cancellation: a failed branch leaves its siblings running and the caller receives a silently partial result.
Forking both children before joining either: wastes a thread slot and doubles join synchronisation points; fork one and compute the other directly.
Using a task granularity that is too fine: creates exponential task counts (O(n^d) at depth d) with negligible leaf work, thrashing the scheduler.
Sharing mutable result objects between sibling tasks: races on the output buffer produce non-deterministic results that vary with scheduling.
Confusing the algorithm's mathematical base case (e.g., size 1) with the parallel cut-off: the parallel cut-off should be much larger (100–10,000 ops) to amortise fork/join overhead.

Wrong move: treating split as free because the recurrence says so -> decomposition copies and re-lays-out subproblem data (Karatsuba, Strassen, FFT per Cao & Liu, ePrint 2016/979), the expansion grows with n and the recursive version loses to the iterative one -> instead charge split/combine their measured cost, or convert to an iterative/in-place form before parallelising.

Wrong move: splitting n into subproblems each nearly as large as n, or into ~n subproblems of size n/c (Neapolitan, Foundations of Algorithms 2.8) -> the recurrence explodes to worse-than-loop time regardless of parallel hardware -> instead reformulate so total subproblem work shrinks, or switch to dynamic programming / a plain scan.

Wrong move: counting single-subproblem recursion (binary search, bisection) as divide-and-conquer and forking it -> there is no forkable width, only overhead -> instead classify it as decrease-and-conquer and use iteration or an explicit stack.
sources: Lea, Doug. 'A Java Fork/Join Framework' (FJTask framework, 2000) — the original Java ForkJoin paper describing work-stealing deque design, efficiency maxims, and optimal expected-time bound O(T1/P + T∞).

Oracle Java Tutorials, 'Fork/Join' (https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/essential/concurrency/forkjoin.html) — official guide with ForkBlur worked example, RecursiveAction vs RecursiveTask choice, and parallelSort() introduction.
Grossman, Dan. 'ForkJoin Framework' (UW CSE 332, SPAC notes) — practical thresholds, warm-up guidance, fork/join ordering constraint, and common performance mistakes.
